sentences.text: Only fragmentary remains of this ancient bird have ever been found.
Despite the incomplete skeleton, scientists estimate it had a wingspan of 5 to 5.5 meters and weighed around 23 kg.
This massive creature differs from its relative Teratornis most obviously in its sheer size.
Detailed bone structure shows the facies articularis ulnaris is slightly more concave than in Teratornis, with a lower dorsal rim than ventral rim.
In Aiolornis, the facies dorsalis is fairly flat along the M. latissimus dorsi attachment and becomes slightly convex near the distal end.
The holotype specimen is around 40% larger than the corresponding bone in Teratornis merriami.
The first material was a cuneiform bone found in Smith Creek Cave, 34 miles north of Baker, Nevada.
The species was first described in 1952 by Howard based on a cuneiform bone.
Campbell, Scott, and Springer moved the species to the new genus Aiolornis in 1999.
The genus name Aiolornis comes from the Greek words aiolus, meaning god of the wind, and ornis, meaning bird.
A partial humerus collected at Quintin Lake in April 1993, about 1 km northeast of Murrieta, California, was referred to the species.
Aiolornis is classified in the family Teratornithidae within the order Cathartiformes.
The order Cathartiformes includes both extinct and extant New World vultures.
Aiolornis lived from the Early Pliocene to the Late Pleistocene.
The time range for Aiolornis is from the Zanclean to the Calabrian, approximately 4.7 to 1.4 million years ago.
Scientists are uncertain if all the material belongs to Aiolornis because the fossils are fragmentary and span a large timespan.
